ety.text: From Latin citrus (“a citron tree, thuja”), probably via Etruscan from Ancient Greek κέδρος (kédros); compare Middle English citurtre, cytyr tre. Thus a possible doublet of cedar.

senses.d: Any of several shrubs or trees of the genus Citrus in the family Rutaceae.

The fruit of such plants, generally spherical, oblate, or prolate, consisting of an outer glandular skin (called zest), an inner white skin (called pith or albedo), and generally between 8 and 16 sectors filled with pulp consisting of cells with one end attached to the inner skin. Citrus fruits include orange, grapefruit, lemon, lime, and citron.
Of, relating to, or similar to citrus plants or fruit.
ex: Its nose is very citrus and fruity.
[…] and his cologne was more citrus than the usual leatherwood floating in formaldehyde.

ety.text: Borrowed from Italian agrume, borrowed from Latin ācrūmen.
From Vulgar Latin or Medieval Latin ācrūmen (“something sour or bitter”), ultimately from Latin ācer (“sharp, sour, bitter”). Cognate to Old French aigrun (“sour fruit”).

ex: São Paulo is the largest city in South America.

senses.d: A settlement granted special status by royal charter or letters patent; traditionally, a settlement with a cathedral regardless of size.
ex: St Davids itself is the smallest city in Great Britain, with a population of less than 2,000.

senses.d: The central business district; downtown.
ex: I'm going into the city today to do some shopping.

senses.d: A large amount of something (used after the noun).
ex: It’s video game city in here!

ety.text: From Middle English citeseyn (“inhabitant of a city or town”), citezein, citisein, from Anglo-Norman citesain (“city-dweller, town-dweller”), citesein, citezein, alteration of citeien from cite (“city”) + -ien (“-ain”) (probable variant of cithein perhaps influenced by dainzain (“denizen”), deinzein), from Old French cite (“city”) + -ien (whence French citoyen), from earlier citet, from Latin civitatem, citatem, from civis. See also city. Displaced native Old English burhsittend and Old English ceasterware.

senses.d: A resident of a city or town, especially one with legally recognized rights or duties.
A legally recognized member of a state, with associated rights and obligations; a person considered in terms of this role.
ex: He is also a citizen of Antigua, because he purchased a home – where he now resides with his family.

senses.d: An inhabitant or occupant: a member of any place.
ex: Diogenes reckoned himself a citizen of the world.
A jellyfish... carries poison cells that can sting other citizens of the sea.

senses.d: A resident of the heavenly city or (later) of the kingdom of God: a Christian; a good Christian.
A civilian, as opposed to a police officer, soldier, or member of some other specialized (usually state) group.
An ordinary person, as opposed to nobles and landed gentry on one side and peasants, craftsmen, and laborers on the other.
A term of address among supporters of the French Revolution in France or elsewhere; (later, dated) a term of address among socialists and communists.
ex: Citizen, I desire nothing more than to get to Paris, though I could dispense with the escort.

senses.d: A notional inhabitant of a software system; an object or a software application.
ex: The HIG delivers Apple's design commandments, the company's definition of what it means to be a good iPhone citizen.

ety.text: From Old French citer, from Latin citare (“to cause to move, excite, summon”), frequentative of ciēre (“to rouse, excite, call”). Sense 4 is the original one.
From the first syllable of citation. Analogous to quote, from quotation.

senses.d: To quote; to repeat, as a passage from a book, or the words of another.
To mention; to make mention of.
To mention by way of explanation.
To list the source(s) from which one took information, words or literary or verbal context.
ex: This Act may be cited as the Boiler Explosions Act, 1882.

senses.d: To summon officially or authoritatively to appear in court.
A citation.
ex: We used the number of cites as a rough measure of the significance of each published paper.

ety.text: Borrowed from Latin citāre (“to summon”), from cieō (“move, stir”). Cognate with English cite.
From Middle English citacioun, from Old French citation, from Latin citātiō. By surface analysis, cite + -ation.

senses.d: An official summons or notice given to a person to appear.
The paper containing such summons or notice.
The act of citing a passage from a text, or from another person, using the exact words of the original text or speech and giving credit to the original by referencing.
An entry in a list of sources from which information was taken, typically following a prescribed bibliographical style; a reference.
An instance of having had one's work cited.
The passage or words quoted; a quotation.
A quotation with attached bibliographical details demonstrating the use of a particular lexical item in a dictionary, especially a dictionary on historical principles.
Enumeration; mention.
ex: It's a simple citation of facts.

senses.d: A reference to decided cases, or books of authority, to prove a point in law.
A commendation in recognition of some achievement, or a formal statement of an achievement.

grp.label: the act of citing a passage from a book
